title: Being and Nothingness
author: Jean-Paul Sartre
target_audience: Readers interested in existentialism and phenomenology
Those exploring questions of consciousness and freedom
Individuals seeking foundational works in continental philosophy
primary_purpose: To provide a phenomenological account of human existence, exploring the nature of consciousness, freedom, and the mechanisms through which individuals construct meaning and identity in a contingent and ultimately ‘absurd’ world.

structure_format.narrative_style: Dense, rigorous, and technical philosophical prose with phenomenological analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into four major parts: (1) The Problem of Nothingness, (2) Being-for-Itself, (3) Being-for-Others, (4) Having, Doing and Being; includes extended introduction and conclusion
features: Systematic exposition of key philosophical concepts
Engagement with preceding philosophical traditions (notably Heidegger and Hegel)

key_concepts_lessons: Human consciousness (‘being-for-itself’) is distinct from inert matter (‘being-in-itself’).
Nothingness is a central characteristic of consciousness, enabling the possibility of negation and absence.
Freedom is fundamental to human existence; humans are ‘condemned to be free’ and fully responsible for their choices.
Bad faith (mauvaise foi) arises when individuals deny their own freedom and responsibility through self-deception.
Personal identity is unstable—shaped by social encounters and the 'gaze' of others.
Authenticity involves acknowledging one’s freedom, facticity, and responsibility in the creation of meaning.
notable_features: Influential conceptions of freedom and the human condition
Exploration of intersubjectivity and the experience of 'the Other'
cultural_historical_context: Written during World War II in occupied France, the book reflects existentialist concerns about authenticity, freedom, and the condition of humanity amidst crisis. Sartre was influenced by Heidegger, Husserl, and existential questions prevailing in early 20th-century philosophy.
reception_impact: Regarded as Sartre’s philosophical magnum opus and a landmark of existentialism
Highly influential in postwar intellectual circles, existential psychology, literature, and political theory
Noted for its complexity and difficulty, inspiring interpretations and debates across humanities disciplines
Inspired subsequent works on subjectivity, selfhood, and social relations
comparable_titles: Being and Time by Martin Heidegger
Existentialism is a Humanism by Jean-Paul Sartre
The Phenomenology of Perception by Maurice Merleau-Ponty
The Ethics of Ambiguity by Simone de Beauvoir
